answer.source_title: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Egypt, Arab Rep.
answer.data_quality_flag: ILO modelled estimate (ILOEST) nowcast for 2025, not a directly observed survey figure; World Bank portal displays the value rounded to whole percent
answer.construct_note: The indicator name 'Employment in agriculture (%)' omits its denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the standard reading. The series also covers ISIC-A (agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing), i.e. slightly broader than agriculture alone — this is the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census. The reference-year 2025 figure is an ILO MODELLED nowcast rather than an observed labour force survey result. An observed national figure sits alongside it: CAPMAS's 2024 annual labour force survey, as reported by the State Information Service (T3), states 'Agriculture and fishing remained the largest employment sectors, engaging 5.594 million workers, representing 18.7 percent of the workforce' — consistent with the modelled 18 and confirming the modelled series is not drifting from national data. A commercial T5 aggregator (statbase.org) reproduces the same ILOSTAT series at 17.52 percent for 2025 and 17.98 for 2024, i.e. the unrounded value behind the World Bank's 18.
answer.quality_evidence: Primary value is from the World Bank WDI portal (T1) sourcing the ILO Modelled Estimates database (ILOEST), accessed January 2026, licensed CC BY-4.0. Cross-checked against an independent, survey-based national source: CAPMAS Annual Labour Force Survey 2024 reported by the Egyptian State Information Service, giving 18.7 percent of the workforce in agriculture and fishing (5.594 million of 29.928 million employed). The two agree to within one percentage point, so the modelled nowcast is not carrying the cell alone.
answer.scale_evidence: National coverage, all employed persons aged 15+. CAPMAS reports total employment of 29.928 million in 2024, of which 5.594 million in agriculture and fishing.
answer.rung_argument: The value itself, not an aggregation, drives the score, so the argument is about whether 18 is the right number for the named construct. (1) A figure exists for Egypt specifically: World Bank/ILOEST publishes 18 for reference year 2025. (2) It is on the correct denominator — the series is titled '% of total employment', which is what the indicator name implicitly requires. (3) It is not an artefact of modelling: the independent CAPMAS 2024 labour force survey puts agriculture and fishing at 18.7 percent of the workforce, so the observed and modelled figures corroborate each other. (4) Against the cut points (lower is better: above 45 = 1, 30-45 = 2, 15-30 = 3, 5-15 = 4, below 5 = 5), 18 clears the 45 and 30 cuts and therefore sits at level 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 would require the agricultural employment share to have fallen below 15 percent of total employment. It has not: the ILO modelled 2025 value is 18 (17.52 unrounded on the same ILOSTAT series per the T5 aggregator), and the observed CAPMAS 2024 survey figure is higher still at 18.7 percent. Neither the modelled nor the survey-based measure is within three points of the 15 cut, and the series is declining by roughly half a point per year, so no published figure supports the next rung.
answer.search_trail: Started with the World Bank WDI country page for SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS filtered to Egypt (T1) — carries Egypt 2025 = 18 in both the 'Selected Countries' and 'All Countries' tables, sourced to ILOEST. Attempted ILOSTAT's own data portal (ilostat.ilo.org/data/) but the retrieved page is a Cloudflare bot-verification interstitial with no data, so the ILO primary could not be quote-verified. Checked CAPMAS microdata catalogue entries for the Annual Labour Force Survey 2020, 2022 and 2024 (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg, T1) — these are metadata/study-description pages only, listing survey objectives and sampling; they contain no employment-by-activity tabulations, so no national figure could be quoted from them. Found the sectoral breakdown instead in the State Information Service report of the CAPMAS 2024 annual LFS (T3): 18.7 percent in agriculture and fishing — used as corroboration in construct_note rather than as the recorded value, since the World Bank T1 series is the register's series. Reviewed FAOSTAT Analytical Briefs 92 and 110 (openknowledge.fao.org, T2) — both give only global and regional shares (26.1 percent globally in 2023; Africa 46 percent) with no Egypt country row in the retrieved text, so they are not evidence for this country. statbase.org (T5) reproduces the ILOSTAT series with unrounded values (17.52 for 2025) but is vendor material and cannot carry a statistic, so it is cited only as context on rounding.

answer.search_trail: Started at the World Bank indicator landing page for NV.AGR.EMPL.KD (Source 1), which carries an all-countries table; located the Egypt, Arab Rep. row with most recent year 2025 and value 8,942.42 and used that as the quote. Cross-checked the same value on the French mirror of the country-filtered page (Source 10, donnees.banquemondiale.org, tier-flagged T5 by domain but substantively the same World Bank series) which shows 8 942,42 for 2025 — used only as corroboration, not as the citation, since the .org data.worldbank.org page is the T1 original. Read both metadata glossary entries (Sources 2 and 3) to pin the sector scope (ISIC Rev. 4 divisions 01-03, i.e. agriculture plus forestry plus fishing) and the price basis (constant 2015 US$), which is what drives the construct_note. Checked the DataBank multi-year table (Source 4) for an Egypt time series, but the retrieved extract truncates alphabetically at Cambodia and never reaches Egypt, so no year-by-year Egypt values could be quoted from it. Checked the WDI table 3.3 extract (Source 5) for 2011 and 2019 Egypt values, but the text truncates mid-row at 'Egypt, Arab' before any figures, so nothing quotable there either. Looked for a national-source alternative: CAPMAS microdata catalogue entry for the Annual Bulletin of Agricultural Income Estimates 2016-2017 (Source 6) is a catalogue record only and publishes no per-worker productivity figure; the Ministry of Agriculture publications listing (Source 9) returns agronomy trial papers, no productivity statistics. Reviewed the two academic/IO sources: the MDPI ARDL paper (Source 7) reports agricultural GDP shares and employment shares (13.6 percent of GDP, 29.2 percent of jobs) but no value added per worker; the IFPRI Egypt SSP working paper (Source 8) discusses productivity gains qualitatively with no per-worker dollar figure. Dead ends recorded rather than filled. No cross-border figures were used.

The **best published match** is the World Bank indicator **NV.AGR.EMPL.KD**, which is **“Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added per worker (constant 2015 US$)”**[1][2]. That means the row’s name **does not exactly match** the published measure if it says only *“Agriculture value added per worker (USD)”*; the published source explicitly includes **forestry and fishing** and specifies **constant 2015 US dollars**[1][3].

For the construct note, the evidence is **on the wrong side of the question**: the published source does **not** state the narrower construct as written, but instead a broader sector scope and a price basis[1][3]. In other words, the closest authoritative source indicates the row should be treated as **agriculture, forestry, and fishing value added per worker in constant 2015 USD**, not a bare “agriculture (USD)” measure[1][2].
